text: Nothing eventful today. I sorted documents into drawers and made dinner at an easy pace.
A phone kept ringing beyond the door. I jumped at every ring and couldn't get to sleep.
I ran into a teacher I hadn't seen in a decade. She recognised me first and pulled me into a hug.
I glued my mother's old cup and saw her handwriting underneath. I sat on the floor until my eyes stopped stinging.
I liked spending the whole day alone in the reading room. It was so still I could hear the pages turn.
The crowd in the square was deafening and everyone sang. I sang too, though I kept looking for a way out.
An email arrived about an error in the paperwork. I paced the room and rushed through checking every file.
When the doctor said the results were fine, I finally breathed out. I'd spent the previous hour gripping my sleeve.
The house emptied after the guests left. I took my time finishing cold tea and missed the children's noise.
My friends showed up with balloons. We laughed and sang in the kitchen until midnight.
I put the phone away and watched a stripe of light on the wall. There was nowhere I needed to hurry to.
Everyone at the meeting gave one-word answers. I watched the clock, hoping I wouldn't have to speak first.
They called in the morning to tell me our dog had died. I couldn't get out of bed for a long time.
Dad quietly tucked a blanket around me while I read, set a cup beside me and left.
I wasn't exactly thrilled, but a walk and good bread made me feel better.
There was no noisy celebration. We stayed home, quietly ate pie and watched lights beyond the window.
I said it was all fine, but clenched my jaw the whole way home after the argument.
The morning felt uncomfortable, but by evening I was painting by the open window without a worry.
Nobody came to the lake. I sat alone until dark, rereading our last message.
My sister helped sort Grandma's things. We cried and laughed as we found her funny little notes.
Construction rattled outside all day. There was nothing to celebrate, so I put my headphones on.
I'd wanted to get out of town alone for ages. On the hill there was only the wind, and it made me smile.
No one answered for an hour, and the intercom kept crackling. I couldn't quietly finish even one page.
We didn't argue today. We put the cupboard together, put the kettle on and talked easily for the first time all week.
What a wonderful day: the bus broke down, I lost my keys, and my boss called me into the office.
Our little choir finished without a mistake. We spoke softly, but I felt quietly delighted.
No one from the team came on my last day. I put the box under my desk and sat until it got dark.
Nothing out of the ordinary. My neighbour brought warm apples and stayed to help clear the table.
The music in the school hall was too loud. But when my nephew finished his dance, we all stood and clapped.
I wasn't crying anymore. I just stared at the shuttered cafe where we used to sit together.
